transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for fitting me in. Well, I guess what finally made me actually make the appointment is that my neck, my shoulders, and my jaw... they're just tight almost all the time now. It feels like I'm constantly bracing for bad news, you know? Even when I'm just sitting at my desk at school. 

I teach 10th-grade history, by the way. Have been for about twenty-five years now. The kids this year, they aren't bad, but getting them to look up from their phones is an absolute nightmare. I had to take up three of them just yesterday during a lesson on the Cold War. You'd think the Cuban Missile Crisis would hold their attention, but no, it's all social media with them. 

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the tightness in my shoulders. Yeah, it doesn't even stop when I get home. I'll be trying to watch TV at night—my wife and I started watching this new British detective show, the one set in the Shetland Islands? The scenery is just incredible, really makes you want to visit Scotland, but even then, sitting on my own couch, I'm just completely tensed up.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or stressed, even when there’s no specific reason for it?

Yeah, exactly. It’s like... there doesn't even have to be a big crisis, my mind just keeps jumping around constantly. I'll be sitting there and suddenly I'm worrying about whether the contractors missed something in the house. We're having the kitchen updated right now—well, just the countertops and the cabinets, really. My wife really wanted quartz instead of granite. The guy at the store said it's less porous, so it doesn't stain if you spill coffee or wine, which makes sense. But the guys installing it just seemed so rushed on Tuesday, you know? 

So I'm stressing about that, and then, before I even finish that thought, I'm worrying about whether my lesson plans are slipping, or if the robotics kids are behind. I sponsor the after-school robotics club, and they're building this little rover thing this year. It's honestly amazing what they can do with a 3D printer and some basic coding. When I was their age, shop class was just building a lopsided birdhouse. But the regional competition is coming up, and the district cut our club funding by ten percent, which is just absurd when you look at the brand new turf they just put on the football field... 

But anyway, where was I? Right, the worrying. My brain just cycles through all of that non-stop, and then I start agonizing over whether I'm disappointing my wife and my family by not keeping everything perfectly under control. It just never really shuts off, even when I'm supposed to be relaxing.
When you feel stressed or anxious, do you notice any other physical symptoms besides the tightness in your neck, shoulders, and jaw—like stomach upset, headaches, or difficulty breathing?

Well, I don't really get stomach aches or anything like that. No trouble breathing, either. Sometimes my head hurts a bit, but honestly, I think that's just from staring at screens too much. Between grading papers on the laptop and trying to figure out the new grading software the district forced on us this year... I swear, the old system was perfectly fine. It was clunky, sure, but at least you knew where everything was. This new one, it takes five clicks just to enter a single homework grade. And they rolled it out right in the middle of midterms! Who does that? The IT guy, bless his heart, he tried to run a training session, but half the staff was out with that awful flu that went around last month. 

I didn't catch the flu, thankfully. My wife makes me drink this elderberry syrup stuff every morning during flu season. Tastes absolutely terrible, like slightly rotten grape juice, but she swears by it. Her sister sells it, actually. She lives down in Florida—Fort Myers area. We went down to visit them a couple of years ago, right before hurricane season started. The humidity down there is just unbelievable. You step outside and your glasses immediately fog up. 

But, uh, no... what were you asking about? Oh, right, stomach stuff. No, my stomach is fine. It's really just the tight shoulders and the jaw.
Do you find it hard to relax or feel restless, like you can't sit still or slow your mind down?

Yeah, exactly that. It's like I'm just... wound up, almost the whole day. Like I'm just sitting there waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Waiting for something else to go wrong. I'll catch myself pacing around the classroom when the kids are doing independent reading, or I'm constantly checking my phone between periods to see if the contractor texted me. 

Speaking of the contractor, he finally sent me a picture of the cabinet hardware this morning. We ordered these brushed nickel pulls, very modern-looking, but the ones he showed me looked more like chrome? I don't know, maybe it was just the lighting in the photo. My wife is very particular about the metals matching. We had this whole debate about whether to mix metals—you know, brass light fixtures with silver cabinet pulls—because apparently that's trendy now. I saw it on one of those home renovation shows we watch. The ones where they buy a completely ruined house and somehow fix it up in three weeks. Which is hilarious, because it's taking our guys three weeks just to put in countertops! 

But yeah, I just... I can't sit still. I'm always moving, always checking things, always feeling like I'm forgetting some disaster that's about to happen.
When you're feeling this constant tension and worry, do you ever notice your heart racing, shaking, or sweating more than usual?

No, my heart doesn't really do that. I don't get the shakes either. And sweating... well, not from the worry, anyway. I mean, I sweat in my classroom, but that's just because the HVAC system in the science wing is completely shot. It's been acting up since October. They keep sending this guy, Gary, from district maintenance, and he just bangs on the vents and tells me the boiler is too old to regulate properly. 

Gary's a great guy, though. He’s actually retiring next year. Says he's going to buy a Class A motorhome and drive out to Yellowstone. I told my wife we should do something like that when I retire—just downsize, get an RV, and hit the road. But she absolutely hates the idea of not having a proper, full-sized bathroom. She says RV bathrooms are basically just closets with a drain. Which, honestly, she has a point. We rented a pop-up camper once back in the late 90s when the kids were little, drove up to the state park. It rained for three days straight. The kids were bouncing off the walls, the dog smelled like wet wool, and the tiny little stove barely worked to heat up a can of soup... 

But, uh, anyway. No. No racing heart or sweating or anything like that. Just the muscle tension and the constant thinking.
Do you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night?

Sleep? No, I actually sleep pretty well, honestly. Once my head hits the pillow, I'm usually out. We did just get a new mattress, though, which helps. One of those memory foam ones that comes completely rolled up in a box. It's wild how they do that, isn't it? They just vacuum-seal a whole king-size bed into a cardboard tube. The delivery guy left it right on the front porch, and it took my son and me an hour to haul the thing up the stairs. 

He's 24 now, my son. Just moved back home. He's trying to find a job in graphic design, but the market is just brutal right now. He sends out twenty resumes a week and hears absolutely nothing back. It's all automated these days, you know? Some computer program screens the resumes before a human even looks at them. I was telling my seniors about that last week, how they need to make sure they use the exact keywords from the job description if they ever want a call back. I really don't know how these kids are going to navigate the workforce. When I got my first teaching job, I just walked into the principal's office with a paper resume, shook his hand, and he hired me on the spot. Mr. Henderson, his name was. He always wore these terrible, loud plaid ties... 

But, sorry, what did you ask me? Right, sleep. Yeah, no, I sleep fine. No problems there.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things, like work, family, or everyday responsibilities, even when there isn't a clear reason to be concerned?

Yeah, all the time. It's like my mind just never stops running through a checklist of everything that could go wrong. I'm constantly jumping from, you know, did the contractors miss something behind the drywall? Because if they did, we're not going to know until it's too late and we have water damage or something. And then I'm worrying about my lesson plans slipping, or if the kids in the robotics club are falling behind schedule for the regional competition. We're supposed to have the chassis built by Friday, but the parts supplier sent the wrong gears. 

Actually, dealing with that parts supplier is a nightmare. It's this company out of Chicago, and their customer service line just puts you in this endless loop of automated menus. "Press 1 for sales, press 2 for support." You press 2, and it just hangs up on you! I spent 45 minutes on hold yesterday while I was eating my lunch in the staff room. Janice, the history teacher, she was in there too, complaining about the new grading software the district is making us use. It's supposed to be more intuitive, but it takes ten clicks just to enter one assignment. Janice is threatening to retire early over it. She's been teaching for thirty years, she remembers when we used to do grades in those green ledger books...

But yeah, it's just this constant feeling that I'm dropping the ball. Like I'm disappointing my wife and my family by not keeping everything perfectly under control, even when I know I'm doing everything I can. It's just exhausting.
Do you feel like the tension and worry you're experiencing is something you can control, or does it feel like it takes on a life of its own?

It definitely takes on a life of its own. I mean, I try to control it. I really do. I'll tell myself to just stop, you know? Just focus on the class in front of me, focus on the lesson. But then one small thought creeps in—like, I'll remember a late invoice for the robotics club, or I'll notice one of my students looking a little lost and falling behind—and suddenly it just sets off this whole chain reaction of what-ifs that I absolutely cannot shut down. 

It's like dominoes. You knock one over and they all just go. We used to set up these massive domino runs when I was a kid. My brother and I would take over the entire living room floor on a Saturday morning. My mom hated it because she couldn't get the vacuum in there. She had this old Hoover upright, weighed about forty pounds, sounded like a jet engine taking off. You don't see vacuums built like that anymore. Everything now is lightweight plastic and runs on batteries. We bought one of those robot vacuums last Christmas—the kind that just wanders around your house on its own? It's supposed to be smart, but the thing gets stuck under the sofa at least twice a week and just beeps until someone rescues it. My wife named it 'Benson' for some reason. She talks to it like it's a pet. 'Oh, Benson's stuck again, go help him out.' 

But, uh, anyway. What was I... right, controlling the worry. No, I can't. Once it starts, it just runs away from me, no matter how hard I try to reel it back in.
Do you feel that your constant worry and muscle tension are significantly affecting your ability to function at work or at home?

Yeah, I'd say it is. I mean, at work, I've really started falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading. And outside of school, I actually had to give up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. 

I usually help build the sets, and we're doing Arsenic and Old Lace this season. It's a great show. My wife actually played one of the aunts when she was in college. She had this incredible vintage dress she found at a thrift shop up in Vermont. We went up to Vermont for our honeymoon, actually. Stayed in this tiny bed and breakfast near Stowe. The owner there, she made these amazing blueberry scones every single morning from scratch. You just can't get real wild blueberries around here, you know? Just those giant, watery ones from the supermarket that turn your whole muffin gray when you bake them. I tried growing my own bushes out by the fence last year, but the deer got to them before they even flowered. The deer in our neighborhood are completely fearless now, they'll walk right up to the front porch and eat the hostas right out of the pots... 

But, I'm sorry, functioning. Right. Yeah, so between the grading piling up on my desk and having to step back from the theater stuff, it's definitely affecting things. I just can't seem to keep all the plates spinning the way I used to.
Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where your heart races, you sweat more than usual, or you feel shaky or trembling, especially when you’re feeling anxious?

No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, my heart doesn't race or anything, and I don't get sweaty or shaky out of nowhere. It's more just this constant, low-level hum of stress, you know? Not like a sudden attack. 

My brother-in-law gets those, though. Panic attacks, I think he calls them. He had one at a family barbecue a couple of years ago. We were all out on my patio—this was right after we put the new flagstone down. Took me three weekends to lay that patio. You have to get the sand base perfectly level, otherwise the stones wobble when you walk on them. And let me tell you, hauling those bags of leveling sand from the home improvement store is a young man's game. I had this old wheelbarrow, the tire was half flat, and I just couldn't get it to hold air. I ended up having to buy one of those solid rubber tires that never go flat. Best investment I ever made. I don't know why they don't just put those on all wheelbarrows straight from the factory. It would save everyone a lot of hassle. Just like how they should put those never-flat tires on bicycles. I remember when I was a kid, patching bike tubes on the front porch with that little kit that smelled like strong rubber cement...

But no, I don't get the racing heart or the shaking. Just the worry.

doctor.question: Do you feel like the tension and worry you're experiencing is something you can control, or does it feel like it takes on a life of its own?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself to stop and focus on the class in front of me, but one small thought—like a late invoice or a student falling behind—sets off a whole chain of what-ifs that I can't shut down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worry is controllable or if it takes on a life of its own, which directly maps to the symptom of Uncontrollable Worry (S057).

patient.answer:
It definitely takes on a life of its own. I mean, I try to control it. I really do. I'll tell myself to just stop, you know? Just focus on the class in front of me, focus on the lesson. But then one small thought creeps in—like, I'll remember a late invoice for the robotics club, or I'll notice one of my students looking a little lost and falling behind—and suddenly it just sets off this whole chain reaction of what-ifs that I absolutely cannot shut down. 

It's like dominoes. You knock one over and they all just go. We used to set up these massive domino runs when I was a kid. My brother and I would take over the entire living room floor on a Saturday morning. My mom hated it because she couldn't get the vacuum in there. She had this old Hoover upright, weighed about forty pounds, sounded like a jet engine taking off. You don't see vacuums built like that anymore. Everything now is lightweight plastic and runs on batteries. We bought one of those robot vacuums last Christmas—the kind that just wanders around your house on its own? It's supposed to be smart, but the thing gets stuck under the sofa at least twice a week and just beeps until someone rescues it. My wife named it 'Benson' for some reason. She talks to it like it's a pet. 'Oh, Benson's stuck again, go help him out.' 

But, uh, anyway. What was I... right, controlling the worry. No, I can't. Once it starts, it just runs away from me, no matter how hard I try to reel it back in.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, which is necessary to distinguish between F45.31 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) and F45.32 (Other Specified Somatic Symptom Disorder).
doctor.question: Do you feel that your constant worry and muscle tension are significantly affecting your ability to function at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've started falling behind on lesson prep and grading, and I gave up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I couldn't keep up with all of it anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms (worry and muscle tension) are significantly affecting the patient's ability to function at work or at home, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I'd say it is. I mean, at work, I've really started falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading. And outside of school, I actually had to give up parts of the community-theater work I usually manage because I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. 

I usually help build the sets, and we're doing Arsenic and Old Lace this season. It's a great show. My wife actually played one of the aunts when she was in college. She had this incredible vintage dress she found at a thrift shop up in Vermont. We went up to Vermont for our honeymoon, actually. Stayed in this tiny bed and breakfast near Stowe. The owner there, she made these amazing blueberry scones every single morning from scratch. You just can't get real wild blueberries around here, you know? Just those giant, watery ones from the supermarket that turn your whole muffin gray when you bake them. I tried growing my own bushes out by the fence last year, but the deer got to them before they even flowered. The deer in our neighborhood are completely fearless now, they'll walk right up to the front porch and eat the hostas right out of the pots... 

But, I'm sorry, functioning. Right. Yeah, so between the grading piling up on my desk and having to step back from the theater stuff, it's definitely affecting things. I just can't seem to keep all the plates spinning the way I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences symptoms of autonomic arousal (e.g., palpitations, sweating, trembling) during episodes of anxiety, which would help differentiate between F45.31 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) and F45.32 (Anxiety Not Otherwise Specified).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where your heart races, you sweat more than usual, or you feel shaky or trembling, especially when you’re feeling anxious?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of panic attacks (racing heart, sweating, trembling), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, my heart doesn't race or anything, and I don't get sweaty or shaky out of nowhere. It's more just this constant, low-level hum of stress, you know? Not like a sudden attack. 

My brother-in-law gets those, though. Panic attacks, I think he calls them. He had one at a family barbecue a couple of years ago. We were all out on my patio—this was right after we put the new flagstone down. Took me three weekends to lay that patio. You have to get the sand base perfectly level, otherwise the stones wobble when you walk on them. And let me tell you, hauling those bags of leveling sand from the home improvement store is a young man's game. I had this old wheelbarrow, the tire was half flat, and I just couldn't get it to hold air. I ended up having to buy one of those solid rubber tires that never go flat. Best investment I ever made. I don't know why they don't just put those on all wheelbarrows straight from the factory. It would save everyone a lot of hassle. Just like how they should put those never-flat tires on bicycles. I remember when I was a kid, patching bike tubes on the front porch with that little kit that smelled like strong rubber cement...

But no, I don't get the racing heart or the shaking. Just the worry.

inference.note: The patient denies experiencing panic attacks or sudden episodes of intense physical symptoms (e.g., heart racing, shaking, sweating), which rules out panic disorder (F41.0) and supports a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder (F45.32). The clinical picture is consistent with GAD, including excessive worry, muscle tension, restlessness, and functional impairment, without features of other anxiety disorders.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, excessive, and uncontrollable worry about multiple domains (e.g., work, family, responsibilities), along with prominent physical symptoms of muscle tension and restlessness. There is clear functional impairment and the symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder such as panic disorder or major depressive disorder. These findings are consistent with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD).
